progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c01 (skeletal and full structural formulas, implied hydrogens, stems meth to oct, endings -ane, -ene, -yne, saturated and unsaturated, longest chain, locants, methyl and ethyl, di-, double-bond locants). Year 11: hydrogen bonding needs an H on O, N or F, and stronger attractions between molecules raise the boiling point; molecular formulas. Not assumed: isomer, functional group, "-ol", cyclo, ether.
progression.startsWith: Hold molecular formula constant. The video opens: Ethanol, the alcohol in this bottle, has the formula C two H six O. Methoxymethane, used as a propellant in some spray cans, has exactly the same formula: two carbons, six hydrogens, one oxygen. Yet ethanol boils at seventy eight degrees, and methoxymethane at about minus twenty five, so it's a gas at room temperature.
progression.stopsAfter: defining structural isomers; classifying a pair as chain, position or functional group isomers with a reason, including saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons; drawing every isomer of a small alkane systematically and rejecting duplicates by naming. No boiling point explanations for branching (chem-m7-c03), no homologous series (chem-m7-c03), no further family naming, no stereoisomers.
progression.nextLesson: how carbon's bonds give hydrocarbons their shapes, and why chain length and branching change boiling points (route chem-m7-c03, "How does carbon bonding explain hydrocarbon properties?").

teaching.task: Ethanol and methoxymethane are made of exactly the same atoms, yet one is a liquid and the other a gas. How can one molecular formula make different molecules, and how do you tell which kind of isomer you are looking at?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) two compounds with the same formula behave differently (1); (2) a molecular formula counts atoms but does not show how they're joined; structural isomers are different compounds (2); (3) the arrangement decides properties: ethanol's O–H lets its molecules hydrogen bond, methoxymethane's oxygen has no hydrogen, so weaker attractions and a lower boiling point (3); (4) chain isomers: same family, different skeleton (4); (5) position isomers: same skeleton and family, group on a different carbon; "-ol" means an O–H group; moving a group can change its reactions (5); (6) functional group isomers: a different family with the same formula; an unsaturated alkene and a saturated ring (6); (7) the group decides the reactions, so the two C₄H₈ isomers behave differently and a test can tell them apart (7); (8) the three-question check, including a non-isomer pair, and why moving a group does not change it (8); (9) finding every isomer by shortening the chain, and why the count stops (9); (10) duplicates are the same molecule drawn differently, so name every structure (10); memory aid (11); two attempts and brief feedback (12 to 15); handoff (16); key notes (17).
teaching.conversationalApproach: ethanol and methoxymethane have exactly the same formula, yet one is a liquid fuel and the other a propellant gas, so the video asks how one molecular formula can make different molecules and how to tell which kind of isomer you are looking at. A formula counts atoms but not how they are joined, and the arrangement changes the properties (ethanol's OH lets its molecules hydrogen bond). The three kinds then come one at a time on the same board: chain isomers change the skeleton within one family (butane and 2-methylpropane), position isomers move the group along the same skeleton (but-1-ene and but-2-ene), and functional group isomers change the group and so the family and its reactions (but-1-ene and cyclobutane). A three-question check classifies any pair, starting with the formula; finding every isomer of C5H12 works systematically by shortening the chain, and duplicates are spotted by tracing the longest chain and naming each structure. The memory aid is "Same formula, different arrangement." Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Ethanol, the alcohol in this bottle, has the formula C two H six O. Methoxymethane, used as a propellant in some spray cans, has exactly the same formula: two carbons, six hydrogens, one oxygen. Yet ethanol boils at seventy eight degrees, and methoxymethane at about minus twenty five, so it's a gas at room temperature. Same atoms, different substances. So how can one formula make different molecules?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "Classify each pair of compounds as chain, position or functional group isomers. (a) pent-1-ene and pent-2-ene (b) pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane (c) cyclopentane and pent-1-ene", with the skeletal formula of each compound beside its name. New compounds (C₅ instead of C₄), all hydrocarbons, one of each type. Crossed mistake: "(a) chain isomers" (the double bond moved; the chain did not change). (A2) "A student draws structures A, B and C and states that they show three different structural isomers of C₅H₁₂. Evaluate the student's statement." A: pentane as a straight zigzag; B: pentane drawn with a right-angle bend (three carbons across, two down); C: 2-methylbutane. Tests the naming check for duplicates and the systematic count. Crossed mistake: "three isomers shown" (B is A drawn differently).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "explore and distinguish the different types of structural isomers, including saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons, including: (ACSCH035); chain isomers; position isomers; functional group isomers" this video starts by holding a molecular formula constant and stops at distinguishing chain, position and functional group isomers. It teaches: a molecular formula counts atoms but does not show how they are joined; structural isomers (same molecular formula, atoms joined in a different order) are different compounds with different names and properties; ethanol against methoxymethane as the opening case, with one Year 11 cause for their different boiling points (hydrogen bonding between ethanol molecules); chain isomers (butane and 2-methylpropane); position isomers (but-1-ene and but-2-ene; propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol, with "-ol" given a one-line meaning); functional group isomers, with "functional group" given a plain meaning (ethanol and methoxymethane; but-1-ene and cyclobutane, a saturated and an unsaturated hydrocarbon with the same formula); a three-question check to classify a pair (same formula? same family? skeleton or position?); a systematic method to find every isomer of a formula (C₅H₁₂: shorten the chain one carbon at a time); spotting duplicates by naming (a bent chain, a methyl on an end carbon, numbering from the wrong end). Not here: why branching lowers boiling points and how chain length changes properties (chem-m7-c03, the next video; one handoff sentence); homologous series (chem-m7-c03; see Decisions); naming alcohols beyond reading "-ol" (chem-m7-c05), aldehydes and ketones (chem-m7-c08b), esters and acids (chem-m7-c09, chem-m7-c10); ether naming (not in the 2017 dotpoints; "methoxymethane" is a name to recognise only); cycloalkane naming rules (only "cyclo means a ring"); stereoisomers, including cis and trans (not in the 2017 syllabus; author note e); counting isomers of C₆ and above; distinguishing an alkene from a cycloalkane by a test (bromine water in chem-m7-c04a and chem-m7-p02).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c01: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; main chain pale blue; branches amber; double bond teal; locants small navy; oxygen red-brown with its hydrogen grey; the what-changed card's changed row lights violet. Board layout (constant): a pair of structures side by side in the centre, the atom tally card between them at the top, the what-changed card at the right when classifying; plates small at the left or right only in scenes 1, 4 and 16. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; one pair on the board at a time. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 21 Oct): `m7-ethanol-fuel-bottle-v1.png` (an amber stoppered glass bottle, half full of pale liquid, no label, no text, no person or hand; 2000 × 2000; hook only, small; Revision 2 no longer brings it back in scene 3), `m7-camping-gas-burner-v1.png` (as in chem-m7-c01; scenes 4 and 16, small). New plate: `m7-aerosol-spray-can-v1.png` (hook only); see Assets. No human figures.
